title: {{NAME}} and the River That Remembered Everything
moral: Healing begins not when we fix what is broken, but when we sit with it long enough to understand what it needs.

pages.content: The River of Memory ran through the heart of the Silverwood, and it was unlike other rivers in one particular way: it remembered. Not in a mystical, vague sense, but specifically, the way a very attentive person remembers: the names of every creature who had ever drunk from it, the season and hour of every storm, the weight and sound of every stone ever rolled along its bed. It told these memories to anyone who listened closely, its voice a constant, layered murmur like a library read aloud all at once. {{NAME}} arrived at the riverbank at dawn, his dove-grey boots finding soft purchase in the moss, and knelt to listen. The river was not well. Its voice was fragmented, stuttering, repeating certain words and dropping others, the way a very old or very frightened thing loses the thread. Upstream, he could see the source of the trouble: the river was running slow, caught behind a new dam of windfall branches and sediment, starving for movement. But he could also sense, in the fragmented murmur, that the problem was more than physical. Something was grieving here.

pages.content: The fairy was barely visible at first, a small intensity of light sitting on a pale stone at the river's edge, her wings still and her chin resting on her knees. Her name was Elver, and she had been the river's companion for a century, sitting with it and listening to its memories and sometimes adding a few of her own. She looked at {{NAME}} with eyes that were ancient and tired and very clear, and said that the dam was not the whole trouble. Three nights ago, the oldest otter who had ever drunk from the river, a creature named Holt who had lived for thirty years beside it, had died, and the river had been losing its voice since then, as if some of its memories had been carried away with him. Grief, Elver said, had many shapes, and one of them was forgetting. {{NAME}} sat beside her and they listened together for a while, and he heard what she meant: beneath the stuttering was a gap, a silence where certain memories had been, now absent. He felt the absence as a specific ache, the way you feel a missing tooth with your tongue, compulsive and sad.

pages.content: Clearing the dam was the easier part, and the animals helped: a family of beavers who had not built it but understood it better than anyone else approached it with professional interest and had it open in forty minutes. The river accelerated gratefully, its voice strengthening, many of the missing words returning, though not all. The gap was still there. But as the water ran clearer and faster, something came: a sound from upstream, high and unwavering, a note of extraordinary purity that ran along the surface of the river like a hand drawn across a singing bowl. {{NAME}} turned. The unicorn stood in the shallows, upstream, her pale gold coat sheened with the early light, her spiral horn touching the surface of the water. Her name was Lune, and she had been walking the Silverwood for longer than the fairies had been counting. The note she was singing held steady. The river's murmur changed. It began to find new words, not replacements for Holt's memories, but something else: the stories other creatures had been carrying about him, their memories of his memories, passed back into the water like a gift.

pages.content: They gathered at the river's widest point, all of them: the beaver family, Elver, Lune, and a dozen animals who had simply come when they heard the river's voice growing stronger, the way neighbours come to a house where music has started. An old badger sat at the very edge of the water and touched his grey nose to the surface, adding something to the river that the river received with a visible ripple. Two herons stood in the shallows in perfect stillness, as if conducting a private ceremony. {{NAME}} waded in up to his knees, the cold water soaking through his grey trousers, and felt the river running against his legs with a force and purpose it had not had an hour ago. He said Holt's name, out loud, into the water, and the river said it back, clearly and with the warmth of a remembered friend. Elver made a small sound above him. Lune lowered her horn and the river surface lit gold for one long, pure moment, and then returned to silver. The gap was not filled, exactly. But it was acknowledged, which is a different and perhaps better thing.

pages.content: The river ran clean and clear as the morning settled in, its voice steady, a little different than before but not lesser, perhaps richer, the way a song sounds different after many people have learned it. Lune waded to the far bank and stood in the full morning sun, her gold coat bright, and the animals who had come arranged themselves along both banks as if settling in for the day. Elver had fallen asleep on a water-smoothed stone, her wings folded like two closed books. The beavers were already discussing improvements to the downstream bank with the purposeful energy of professionals who have completed one job and are immediately interested in the next. {{NAME}} climbed out of the water and sat on a warm mossy root, his damp trousers steaming faintly in the sun. He leaned back and let the warmth find him. The river talked on beside him, its voice full and layered, carrying names he did not know and some he did. His breathing slowed to match its rhythm. He was nearly asleep when the river said a new name, clearly and with great affection. His own. He smiled without opening his eyes, and the river carried the sound of it far downstream, into the silver distance.
